precmed: Estimation and validation of heterogeneous treatment effects

Source: R/precmed-package.R
precmed-package.Rd

Tools for estimating population-average and covariate-conditional treatment effects in randomized and observational studies with binary, count, or time-to-event outcomes. Causal interpretation requires appropriate identification and modeling assumptions.

Details

Use atefit() to estimate population-average treatment effects. Use catefit() to develop conditional treatment-effect scores and catecv() to evaluate scores using cross-validation. Estimating a population-average effect and validating a conditional treatment-effect score are distinct tasks. Use diagnostics() to inspect available diagnostics and subgroup_estimates() to extract subgroup results.

Outcomes and effect scales

For binary outcomes, atefit() estimates the population-average risk difference (treatment 1 minus treatment 0). For count outcomes it estimates a population-average rate ratio. For survival outcomes at a chosen horizon, it estimates a restricted mean time lost ratio, cumulative hazard ratio, and event risk difference (treatment 1 minus treatment 0). The CATE scores describe effects conditional on covariates; their scales depend on the outcome. See atefit and catefit for details.

The question and the models

In observational studies, treatment groups may differ in baseline characteristics that also affect outcomes. A treatment model estimates propensity scores, the probabilities of treatment assignment given covariates. An outcome model predicts the outcome given treatment and covariates. These models can be used to adjust for measured covariates when estimating treatment effects. For survival outcomes, a censoring model supplies probabilities used for inverse probability of censoring weighting.

What does doubly robust mean?

atefit() uses doubly robust estimators of population-average treatment effects for binary, count, and survival outcomes. These estimators combine outcome and treatment models so that, under the required causal identification and regularity assumptions, they are consistent if either the outcome model or the treatment model is correctly specified. Both models may be correct. Double robustness does not protect against unmeasured confounding, poor treatment overlap, or misspecification of both models. The property is asymptotic and does not guarantee negligible bias in a finite sample. For survival outcomes, it also does not protect against a misspecified censoring model. If an out-of-range restricted mean survival estimate triggers an outcome-model fallback, the substituted estimate does not retain the doubly robust guarantee. See atefit for details.

Online guides and vignettes

The package website provides a quick start, an introduction to doubly robust methods, and all vignettes, including examples and methodological details for different outcomes. These resources are available online; the vignettes are not included in the CRAN package build.

Examples

# A small illustrative example; use more bootstrap replicates in practice.
dat <- simulate_binary(n = 400, seed = 2026)
fit <- atefit(response = "binary", data = dat,
              cate.model = y ~ age + previous_treatment,
              ps.model = trt ~ age + previous_treatment,
              n.boot = 20, seed = 2026)
coef(fit)
#> risk.difference 
#>      -0.1420822 
diagnostics(fit)
#> [1] method    split     iteration group     subgroup  type      measure  
#> [8] message  
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
